Paper: Rezende and Mohamed (2015), [Variational Inference with Normalizing Flows](https://arxiv.org/abs/1505.05770).
A normalizing flow transforms a simple distribution through invertible maps while accounting for the change in probability density.
This paper uses that mechanism to construct more expressive approximate posteriors for variational inference.

## Problem

A tractable approximate posterior, such as a diagonal Gaussian in a [VAE](vae.qmd), can fail to represent correlations, asymmetry, or multiple regions of high posterior density.
Increasing the flexibility of the encoder network does not remove the restrictions of its output distribution family.
The desired distribution must remain easy to sample and evaluate so that it can still enter the variational objective. [Paper, §§1–2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1505.05770#page=1).

## Previous attempts

Mean-field variational inference gains tractability by restricting the posterior family.
More elaborate inference procedures can improve the approximation but add computational cost or require specialised estimators.
Normalizing flows instead start from a tractable base density and compose transformations whose effect on density can be computed. [Paper, §§2–3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1505.05770#page=2).

## Proposed solution

First consider a generative map $x=f(z)$, where $z\sim p_0$ and $f$ is a differentiable bijection with a nonsingular Jacobian.
The model density is

$$
  p_\theta(x)
  =p_0(f^{-1}(x))\left|\det J_{f^{-1}}(x)\right|.
$$

At $x=f(z)$, this is equivalently

$$
  p_\theta(f(z))
  =\frac{p_0(z)}{|\det J_f(z)|}.
$$

Expanding a small region spreads its probability mass over more volume, so the density decreases.
For the scalar example $x=2z$, the density is $p_\theta(x)=p_0(x/2)/2$.
The forward determinant divides density; the inverse determinant multiplies it. [Paper, Eq. (5)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1505.05770#page=4).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Derivation: preserve probability while changing volume"}

Corresponding infinitesimal regions must have equal probability:

$$
  p_\theta(x)\,dx=p_0(z)\,dz.
$$

The local volume transformation is $dx=|\det J_f(z)|\,dz$.
Substitution gives the denominator in the forward-map formula.
Differentiating $f^{-1}(f(z))=z$ gives

$$
  J_{f^{-1}}(f(z))J_f(z)=I.
$$

Taking determinants proves that the two absolute determinants are reciprocals.
If the named map instead runs from data to latent space, its determinant appears with the opposite sign in the log-density formula because the map direction has changed.

:::

For a composition $z_k=f_k(z_{k-1})$ starting from $z_0\sim q_0$, the transformed density satisfies

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  \log q_K(z_K)&=\log q_0(z_0)\\
  &\quad-\sum_{k=1}^{K}\log|\det J_{f_k}(z_{k-1})|.
  \end{aligned}
$$

The paper applies this chain to an approximate posterior $q_K(z_K\mid x)$.
Its base distribution and transformation parameters may depend on the observed example $x$ through an inference network. [Paper, Eqs. (6)–(8) and §4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1505.05770#page=4).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Derivation: insert the flow posterior into the ELBO"}

Write $d_k=\log|\det J_{f_k}(z_{k-1})|$, with conditioning on $x$ implicit.
Changing the expectation from the transformed variable to its base sample gives

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  B(x)=\mathbb E_{q_0}\bigg[
  &\log p_\theta(x,z_K)-\log q_0(z_0)\\
  &+\sum_{k=1}^{K}d_k\bigg].
  \end{aligned}
$$

The determinant sum has a plus sign here because the ELBO subtracts $\log q_K$.
That sign does not contradict the minus sign in the transformed-density formula.
The generative model still evaluates its joint density at the final latent sample $z_K$.

:::

One concrete construction is the planar transformation

$$
  f(z)=z+u\,h(w^\top z+b).
$$

Its Jacobian is a rank-one update of the identity, giving

$$
  \det J_f(z)=1+u^\top\psi(z),
$$

$$
  \psi(z)=h'(w^\top z+b)w.
$$

The determinant can therefore be evaluated in linear time in the latent dimension, while additional parameter constraints ensure invertibility. [Paper, §4 and Appendix A](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1505.05770#page=5).

## Evidence

The paper visualises increasingly expressive transformed densities on synthetic target distributions and evaluates flow posteriors in deep latent Gaussian models.
These experiments investigate the benefit of posterior flexibility within the chosen models, rather than establishing that every invertible architecture is efficient for every task. [Paper, §6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1505.05770#page=6).

## Limitations

Invertibility alone does not guarantee cheap density evaluation: the needed map direction and Jacobian determinant must also be tractable.
For variational inference, the sampled base variable is already known, so evaluating the posterior at that transformed sample can avoid solving an inverse problem.
This differs from evaluating a standalone flow density at an arbitrary supplied observation.
The model density is the density induced by the learned map, not automatically the unknown data density.

## Connections

[Flow matching](flow-matching.qmd) trains continuous normalizing flows by regressing velocity fields.
Finite compositions and continuous flows belong to a connected family; flow matching is a training method, not a claim that continuous models cease to be normalizing flows.
[Score-based models](score-based-models.qmd) provide a probability-flow ODE that creates another connection between diffusion and continuous density transformations.
